name: Full-body training

card.summary: Resistance workouts that train the whole body in each session, usually two to four times a week, to build muscle and a fuller physique with less gym time.
card.note: General fitness practice; individuals with medical conditions are typically advised to consult a clinician.

quick.overview:
Full-body training means working most major muscle groups in every session rather than dividing them across days. For looks, the payoff is more muscle size and strength in the shoulders, back, chest, arms and legs, built on a schedule that suits people who can only get to the gym two or three times per week.

A randomized trial in 67 untrained people compared a split routine with a full-body routine for eight weeks. Both groups gained strength and muscle thickness with no significant difference between them, and the authors concluded results were similar when weekly set volume was equal.
quick.how: People pick compound exercises such as squats, presses, rows and pull-ups, and repeat the session two to four times per week with rest days between. On looksmax.org, users ask for short routines of 45 minutes or less, or for two to three weekly sessions, and some use bodyweight versions at home.
quick.risks: Risks are those of resistance training generally: soreness, overuse or technique-related injury, and fatigue if recovery is short. Full-body days can be tiring when volume per session is high.

lead: Full-body training is a way of organising resistance workouts so that most or all major muscle groups are trained in every session, as opposed to splits such as upper/lower, push/pull/legs or the 'bro' split, which assign different muscles to different days.[3] A typical full-body week has two to four sessions on non-consecutive days, each built around compound movements such as squats, presses, rows, pull-ups and deadlifts.

For appearance, the point is muscle: larger shoulders, a wider back, fuller chest and arms and stronger legs are the visible result of progressive resistance training, and full-body scheduling is one way of delivering the weekly volume needed for them.[7] Because each muscle is stimulated several times a week, and because the schedule needs only two or three gym visits, it is popular with beginners and with people who have limited time. On looksmax.org, users ask for routines of two to three sessions weekly or of 45 minutes or less.[4][5]

Research comparing full-body and split programmes has largely found similar strength and muscle-thickness gains when weekly set volume is matched, including an eight-week randomized trial in 67 untrained adults.[1] A meta-analysis of training frequency concluded that training each muscle at least twice a week produced more growth than once a week when volume was equated.[10] A 2024 randomized trial in well-trained men reported greater fat-mass loss with a full-body arrangement than with a split at the same volume.[11]

chain: Train every major muscle group each session

angle.text: Each session trains the whole body, so lifters can reach their weekly volume in two to four sessions. That fits busy schedules and gives repeated growth stimulus to each muscle.

paras: Common ways to arrange resistance training include full-body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and body-part splits; a split simply defines which muscles are trained on which days of the week.[3] A full-body session combines exercises for the legs, back, chest, shoulders and arms in one workout and repeats it on alternate days, so that every muscle is trained each time.

Because each session covers so many muscles, per-muscle volume in one session is usually modest, often a few hard sets per movement pattern, and the weekly total comes from repetition across sessions. Many programmes lean on multi-joint lifts that work several muscle groups at once, which is how a short session can touch the whole body. Lifters also use supersets and shorter rests to compress a session, an approach reviewed in a 2026 Frontiers in Public Health perspective on time-efficient ways to meet muscle-strengthening guidelines.[12]

Resistance training itself has a long history. Wikipedia traces progressive overload to the story of Milo of Croton, notes Galen's 2nd-century description of exercises with halteres, and records the move from sand-filled globe barbells to plate-loaded barbells by the end of the 19th century, weightlifting's debut at the 1896 Athens Olympics, and the arrival of machines in gyms during the 1960s.[3]

Physique-focused training developed alongside bodybuilding. Eugen Sandow, promoted as the father of modern bodybuilding, staged muscle-display shows and sold early mass-market exercise equipment, and organised the 1901 Great Competition in London; the Weider brothers founded the IFBB in 1946, and magazines of the 1950s and 1960s spread training and nutrition principles.[8] Body-part splits became closely associated with competitive bodybuilding, while whole-body sessions remained the default for strength-sport beginners. Mark Rippetoe and Lon Kilgore's Starting Strength, first published in 2005, built a beginner programme around a handful of barbell compound lifts and a limited number of assistance exercises, and is a widely cited example of whole-body barbell training.[9]

Interest in the format among looksmaxxing users is mostly practical rather than ideological: it comes up when people with jobs, school or travel want a physique programme that fits few sessions per week.

Wikipedia's overview of muscle hypertrophy describes mechanical tension as the currently accepted main driver of growth, acting through signalling such as mTOR to increase muscle protein synthesis, and notes that early strength gains in beginners come largely from neural adaptations before measurable size changes.[7] It lists frequency, intensity and total volume as variables that directly affect hypertrophy, and says protein intakes up to about 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day help increase strength and size according to a cited meta-analysis.[7]

Full-body scheduling is one way to change how that volume is distributed. Spreading sets across more days means each muscle is stimulated more often and no single session needs very high volume for one body part. Strength-training references report that training a muscle twice a week produces more growth than once, that the benefit of a third weekly session is unresolved, and that when total volume is equal frequency has no clear effect on strength gains.[3]

People adapt full-body training in several ways. Two-day versions suit those with the least time; three-day versions on alternate days (for example Monday, Wednesday, Friday) are the classic beginner layout; four-day versions are sometimes alternated between two session types, such as an A and a B workout with different lifts.[3] Some lifters cycle emphasis between sessions, giving a heavy, a moderate and a lighter day to the same movements.

Home and equipment-free variants substitute push-ups, pull-ups, dips, squats and ab-wheel work for gym lifts. A looksmax.org guide posted during gym closures in 2020 suggested picking one or two exercises per muscle group, and said such workouts help maintain muscle if not add new gains.[6] Another poster listed a simple home circuit of pull-ups, ab-wheel rollouts and push-ups.[6]

Beginner barbell programmes in the style of Starting Strength alternate two whole-body sessions built on the squat, press, bench press, deadlift and power clean.[9] Intermediate lifters sometimes move to upper/lower or push/pull/legs splits when they want more volume per muscle in each session; the 2021 trial suggests the choice is a matter of schedule preference when weekly sets are equal.[1]

Strength-training references report that, for muscle growth, training a muscle twice per week is better than once, while the benefit of a third weekly session is unresolved; when total volume is equal, frequency does not change strength gains.[3] The 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger, covering ten studies, found a larger hypertrophy effect size for higher training frequency (0.49 versus 0.30) and concluded that major muscle groups should be trained at least twice weekly, with the three-times-weekly question unresolved.[10]

The 2021 randomized trial in untrained people reached a similar conclusion for hypertrophy and strength when comparing a twice-weekly split with a four-times-weekly full-body routine at equal weekly set volume.[1]

On looksmax.org, users who want a good physique but have little time ask for efficient full-body programmes. One poster wanted to cut a 75-minute session to 45 minutes using supersets and drop sets, proposing overhead press, dips, seated cable row, leg press, wrist roller, calf raises and a face-pull and ab superset; a reply from another member called the plan pretty good and suggested adding abs and doing dips and wrist rolling at home.[4]

Another poster said they could not get to the gym four or five days a week and asked for a full-body workout two to three times weekly, listing push-ups, dips, bench press, shoulder press, deadlift, rows, curls or pull-ups and abs; one reply suggested a 5x5 programme with leg curls and extensions and added dumbbell lateral raises, saying they add shoulder width.[5] Shoulder width, a V-taper and overall muscularity are physique goals commonly discussed in these threads, and the posts show full-body routines framed as a way to pursue them on a constrained schedule.[4][5]
The same forum shares equipment-free versions for people without gym access.[6]

Risks are those of resistance training in general. Wikipedia notes that poor form can cause injury and that the NSCA recommends warm-ups, though evidence that warm-ups reduce injury is limited; the Valsalva manoeuvre used by some powerlifters is described as risky for people with high blood pressure or a tendency to faint.[3] Full-body sessions with several heavy compound lifts can be fatiguing, and recovery between sessions matters, which is one reason the format is usually done on non-consecutive days.[3] Resistance training is considered safe for children with proper design and supervision and for older adults with adapted intensity, according to the same overview.[3]

In a randomized trial of 67 untrained adults, a split routine (A/B, twice per week) was compared with a full-body routine (four times per week) over eight weeks. Both improved bench press and squat strength and the thickness of the elbow extensors, elbow flexors and quadriceps, with no significant difference between groups; the authors concluded that twice or four times weekly gives similar results at equal weekly set volume.[1]

A 2024 randomized trial in 23 well-trained men assigned participants to a full-body group (each muscle trained five days per week) or a split group (each muscle once per week) with the same 75 weekly sets for eight weeks. The full-body group lost more whole-body fat mass by DXA (a 0.775 kg reduction versus a 0.317 kg increase), and the authors concluded that full-body training reduced fat mass more than the split.[11]

A 12-week full-body resistance programme in Slovenian Armed Forces personnel studied vertical jumping with and without military equipment.[2] A 2016 meta-analysis of frequency studies is described above.[10]

timeline.event: Weightlifting appears at the first modern Olympic Games in Athens.[3]
Eugen Sandow organises the Great Competition at the Royal Albert Hall in London, an early physique contest.[8]
Joe and Ben Weider found the IFBB, helping spread bodybuilding training through magazines in following decades.[8]
Exercise machines are gradually introduced into gyms.[3]
The documentary Pumping Iron publicises bodybuilding.[8]
Starting Strength by Mark Rippetoe and Lon Kilgore is first published.[9]
Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger publish a meta-analysis of resistance-training frequency and hypertrophy.[10]
Randomized trial compares split and full-body routines in 67 untrained adults.[1]
Randomized trial in well-trained men reports greater fat-mass loss with full-body than split training.[11]
Perspective in Frontiers in Public Health reviews time-saving strategies for muscle-strengthening guidelines.[12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, full-body routines are discussed as time-efficient ways to build a physique, usually by people balancing gym time against other commitments.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: Two to three full-body sessions a week are enough for a good physique
claims.believers: Posters with limited time ask for or share short full-body plans that fit that schedule.[4][5]
claims.experts: The 2021 randomized trial found similar strength and thickness gains between full-body and split training at equal weekly volume, and a frequency meta-analysis supports at least two sessions per muscle per week.[1][10]

claims.claim: Home bodyweight full-body workouts maintain muscle
claims.believers: A poster says equipment-free workouts keep your current physique even if they do not add new gains, provided calories are not in deficit.[6]
claims.experts: No trial cited here tests bodyweight-only maintenance in this population; resistance training in general is studied.[3]

claims.claim: A 45-minute session can cover the whole body using supersets
claims.believers: One poster proposes cutting from 75 to 45 minutes with compound lifts and supersets.[4]
claims.experts: A 2026 perspective describes supersets and minimal-dose approaches as time-saving ways to meet strengthening guidelines.[12]

claims.claim: Full-body training burns more fat than a split
claims.believers: Forum posters generally frame full-body routines as efficient, though fat-loss comparisons with splits are not a focus of those threads.[4]
claims.experts: A 2024 randomized trial of 23 trained men reported greater fat-mass loss with full-body than split training at equal volume; it was a small, eight-week study.[11]

claims.claim: Adding lateral raises and rows builds shoulder and back width
claims.believers: A forum reply recommends dumbbell laterals to add shoulder width to a full-body plan.[5]
claims.experts: Resistance-training references say growth depends on training volume and progressive overload for the muscle in question.[3][7]

claims.claim: Training a muscle only once a week limits growth compared with twice
claims.believers: Full-body advocates say frequent exposure keeps muscles stimulated.[5]
claims.experts: A meta-analysis of ten studies found twice-weekly training of a muscle gave more hypertrophy than once weekly with volume equated.[10]
